issues.legal_issue: The statutory power to exempt buildings from rent-control protections is not an unconstitutional delegation of legislative power or a violation of equality guarantees.
material_facts: The legislation authorized the government to exempt a particular building or class of buildings from rent-control provisions.
Earlier decisions had upheld comparable exemption powers, and an earlier decision had upheld the same statutory power against delegation and equality challenges.
issues.conclusion: The statutory exemption power is valid and does not suffer from excessive delegation or violate the equality guarantee.
issues.legal_principle: The Court relied on P. J. Irani v. The State of Madras, which upheld a comparable exemption power, State of Madhya Pradesh v. Kanhaiyalal, which likewise upheld an exemption power, and Sadhu Singh v. The District Board, Gurdaspur, which held that this statutory power did not involve excessive delegation or violate Article 14. The relevant provision was section 3 of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, as modified for the territory.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_rent_control: A constitutional challenge is brought against the power to exempt buildings from rent-control protections.
predicates.legislation_authorizes_executive_exempti: The legislature authorizes the executive to exempt buildings or classes of buildings from rent-control protections.
predicates.comparable_exemption_powers_have_been_up: Earlier court decisions have upheld comparable executive exemption powers.

issues.definition: When a constitutional challenge concerns a legislatively authorized executive power to exempt buildings and comparable powers have been upheld, the exemption power is valid.

issues.legal_issue: A temporary exemption for new buildings that encourages additional housing is consistent with the tenant-protection policy of rent-control legislation and is not discriminatory when the classification has a reasonable connection to that purpose.
material_facts: The notification exempted new buildings from rent-control protections for a limited period.
The administration stated that the exemption was intended to encourage investment in new construction and increase the supply of housing.
The Court found that additional housing could mitigate hardship for tenants and that the temporary exemption balanced landlords' and tenants' interests.
The distinction between exempt and non-exempt buildings was connected to the aim of creating additional housing.
issues.conclusion: The exemption was not outside the object and policy of the legislation and was not discriminatory, arbitrary, or unreasonable.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that a statute's object and policy are not always confined strictly to its preamble and express provisions. The broader policy of the rent-control legislation was to mitigate tenant hardship, and encouraging new construction could advance that policy by increasing housing supply. The temporary classification had a reasonable nexus to that objective and did not violate Article 14. The relevant provisions were section 3 of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, as modified for the territory, and Article 14 of the Constitution.

predicates.challenge_to_exemption_as_inconsistent_o: A challenge alleges that an exemption from rent-control protections is inconsistent with the law's purpose or discriminates between buildings.
predicates.rent_law_aims_to_mitigate_tenant_hardshi: The rent-control scheme is intended generally to mitigate hardship faced by tenants.
predicates.temporary_exemption_encourages_new_housi: The executive grants a limited-duration exemption to encourage investment in new housing construction.
predicates.exempted_class_has_reasonable_nexus_to_a: The buildings given the exemption form a class reasonably connected to increasing the supply of housing.

issues.definition: A temporary exemption that encourages new housing and reasonably advances a rent law's tenant-hardship mitigation aim is consistent with that law's policy and is not discriminatory.

issues.legal_issue: An administrator of a Union Territory may exercise the Central Government's exemption power when authorized to discharge the relevant governmental functions, and actions covered by a validating law remain effective.
material_facts: The rent-control law was extended to the Union Territory with modifications.
A presidential direction authorized the territory's administrator to exercise and discharge governmental powers and functions under laws extended to the territory.
The applicable definition of the Central Government included the territory's administrator acting within the authority conferred under Article 239.
The Union of India did not dispute the administrator's authority, and the extension legislation validated notifications issued or purportedly issued under the rent-control law.
issues.conclusion: The administrator had authority to issue the notifications, and the applicable validating provision confirmed the validity and effectiveness of the notifications it covered.
issues.legal_principle: Article 239(1) permits administration of a Union Territory through an appointed administrator. Section 3(8)(b)(iii) of the General Clauses Act, 1897, includes the administrator within the meaning of the Central Government for Union Territory administration when acting within the authority conferred under Article 239. Section 4 of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act (Extension to Chandigarh) Act, 1974 validated covered prior actions and notifications. The Court also relied on Uttam Bala Ravankar v. Asstt. Collector of Customs & Central Excise, Goa, which applied the General Clauses Act definition to uphold an administrator's notification.

rule.if: challenge_to_administrator_issued_exemption_notice and rent_law_extended_to_union_territory and administrator_authorized_to_exercise_relevant_governmental_powers and administrator_included_in_central_government_definition and validating_law_covers_the_notice

predicates.challenge_to_administrator_issued_exempt: A challenge is brought against an exemption notice issued by a Union Territory administrator.
predicates.rent_law_extended_to_union_territory: The relevant rent-control law has been extended to the Union Territory.
predicates.administrator_authorized_to_exercise_rel: The administrator has been authorized to exercise the relevant governmental powers under laws extended to the territory.
predicates.administrator_included_in_central_govern: The applicable general legal definition includes the administrator within the Central Government when acting within the granted authority.
predicates.validating_law_covers_the_notice: A validating law covers the notice or the action by which it was issued.

issues.definition: When an administrator issues an exemption notice under an extended law, is authorized to exercise the relevant powers, falls within the applicable governmental definition, and is covered by a validating law, the notice is authorized and validated.

issues.legal_issue: An exemption notification does not operate retrospectively to cover buildings that had already met the relevant qualifying criteria before the notification was issued unless its language clearly indicates that result or the surrounding circumstances establish that intent.
material_facts: The rent-control law applied to buildings existing before the exemption notification was issued.
The notification's wording did not clearly state that it covered buildings that had already met the relevant connection or occupancy criteria.
The notification was intended to encourage construction of new buildings, and the Court found no compelling reason to remove existing tenants' statutory protection.
Landlords sought to apply the exemption to buildings whose qualifying connection or occupancy had occurred before the notification.
issues.conclusion: The exemption applied only to buildings whose relevant connection or occupancy occurred on or after the notification; buildings that had already met the relevant criteria remained subject to the rent-control law.
issues.legal_principle: Substantive laws generally operate prospectively, and there is a presumption against retrospectivity where vested rights or obligations are affected, unless legislative intent is clear and compelling. Retrospective operation may follow from express words or language that necessarily implies it; where the language is unclear, surrounding circumstances must be considered. The Court discussed Om Prakash Gupta v. Dig Vajendrapal Gupta, noting that it concerned a different statutory provision and that its judgment had been set for rehearing; it also noted the differing approaches in Ratan Lal Shinghal v. Smt. Murti Devi and Shri Ram Saroop Rai v. Smt. Lilavati. Strawboard Manufacturing Co. Ltd. v. Gupta Mill Workers Union, Dr. Indramani Pyarelal Gupta v. W. R. Nathu, and Income-tax Officer, Alleppey v. M. C. Ponnoose were also referred to in relation to retrospective operation. The Court held that the notification had to be interpreted on its own language and circumstances.

predicates.challenge_to_retroactive_application_of_: A proceeding challenges the retrospective application of a rent-control exemption notification.
predicates.rent_control_applied_to_buildings_before: Rent-control protections already applied to the buildings before the exemption notice was issued.
predicates.notice_language_does_not_clearly_cover_p: The notice does not clearly express an intent to exempt buildings that had already met its qualifying criteria.
predicates.exemption_aims_to_encourage_future_const: The exemption was intended to encourage construction of new buildings after its issuance.

issues.definition: If rent-control protections already applied, the notice does not clearly cover pre-existing buildings, and the exemption was intended to encourage future construction, those pre-notice buildings are not exempted.
